title: Fight Club
synopsis: Insomnia, soap, a basement, and a man in the mirror who has finally caught up to you.

nodes.text: Tuesday is testicular cancer in a church basement with bad coffee. You give a false name and a false diagnosis, and a man with real tumours holds on to you and cries into your collar, and afterward you sleep for nine hours for the first time since spring. That's the trade: other people's dying, converted into your rest. Nobody in the circle has done anything wrong except you.

choices.consequence: Something comes out of you that isn't performed, and the man holding you can't tell the difference, and you can't decide whether that makes it better.
You do the breathing and the face and the appropriate noises. Stolen comfort works exactly as well as the real thing, which is the year's most alarming discovery.

nodes.text: She turns up at melanoma, then at blood parasites, and she smokes through the guided meditation. She's a liar and you're a liar and her lie ruins yours — you can't get to the crying with a witness in the room. You hate her immediately and very specifically, and there's a strange lightness inside the hate, like recognising a relative in an airport.

choices.consequence: You corner her by the urn and divide the week like a custody arrangement. She takes bowel and TB and leaves you the good ones, and she is already winning.
You start sitting where you can watch the back of her head. The insomnia comes straight back and you blame her for it, and you're mostly wrong.

nodes.text: Seat 27B: a soap salesman in a red leather jacket with a bag identical to yours. He says everything on this aircraft is single-serving, friendships included. He's funny enough that the people in front turn round. He talks about your job — recall formulas, how many bodies make a repair worth doing — and he has it exactly right, and you never told him. He gives you a card.

choices.consequence: You put it in your wallet behind the airline miles, and you'll dial it that same night from a phone booth, drunk, with nowhere to sleep.
You leave it in the seat pocket and it's in your coat at baggage claim, and you don't wonder how, because wondering how would be the end of it.

nodes.text: Fifteenth floor, and seven years of careful assembly is on the pavement in the rain — the shelving unit, the good glassware, the sofa you thought about for a month. Gas leak, the doorman says. You were insured. You stand on the street with a suitcase and a phone card and find you aren't frightened, and the not being frightened ought to worry you far more than it does.

choices.consequence: You dial him twice and hang up before it rings, and then he calls you, which you should ask about and never do. He tells you where the bar is.
You get halfway through her number and stop, because she would ask real questions. You make the easier call and tell yourself it was the only one available.

nodes.text: Parking lot behind the Lucky at closing time, and he asks you to hit him as hard as you can. You have never hit anybody. You go for the ear because you're embarrassed. He laughs, knocks you sideways off a car, and you sit down in the gravel with your mouth full of blood and your heart going like a trapped bird, and something you've carried since your father left sets itself down for a minute.

choices.consequence: It lands wrong and hurts your wrist and it is still the most present you have felt in a decade. That feeling is the hook, and the hook is set.
You say no three times and then do it anyway, and the fact that you had to be talked into it is the detail you'll edit out when you tell the story later.

nodes.text: By March there are forty men in a bar cellar on Paper Street and a set of rules recited like a catechism. Two shirtless men, no shoes, it ends when somebody taps out. The first rule and the second rule are the same rule, and the men love saying them, and the loving is the whole point — it's the first thing most of them have belonged to since school. Nobody notices they've stopped choosing.

choices.consequence: You say the rules in the dark with your voice buried inside forty voices, and there is no lonelier way to feel less alone.
You reach the stairs and come back down, because upstairs is a rented room and a job and nobody who would notice. That is the entire recruitment pitch.

nodes.text: The house has one bathroom and the door doesn't latch properly. You hear her in there with him — water, and laughing, and then a sound that isn't laughing — and you stand in the corridor with a mug going cold in your hand. In the morning she comes downstairs and looks straight at you as though you were the one who owed an explanation. In a way nobody understands yet, you are.

choices.consequence: You stand there four minutes hating both of them and can't work out which one you're jealous of. Neither answer is one you want to be true.
You go up to your room and put a pillow over your head like a kid. Whatever you refuse to look at directly gets to keep operating inside your house.

nodes.text: Behind a clinic in the valley there's a dumpster, and in the dumpster there are bags, and on the kitchen stove it renders down over two days until the whole street smells of it. You cut it into bars and wrap them in brown paper and department stores pay twenty dollars each. He thinks this is the funniest thing that has ever happened. You laugh too. You're the one who scrubs the pot.

choices.consequence: You take the money and buy groceries and a phone line, and it works, and the joke curdles somewhere around the fourth delivery.
You call it grotesque and he agrees enthusiastically, and you carry the bags to the car regardless. Objecting out loud is how you keep believing you're separate from it.

nodes.text: The man who owns the building comes down with two of his people and a bat, and Tyler stands in front of forty men and lets himself be beaten in the face until he isn't recognisable, then laughs up at him with his teeth full of blood until the man is too disgusted to continue. It works. The room reads it as courage. You watch someone make himself repulsive on purpose and call it winning.

choices.consequence: You do what the room does — get in the way, take some of it — and the fear you should be feeling arrives an hour late and much quieter than it should.
You put your palms out and step back, and forty men see you do it, and nobody says a word, and every one of them remembers.

nodes.text: The assignments start small — a fight picked with a stranger, a sign moved — and then he's handing out car keys and address lists. Yours is a franchise coffee outlet and a jug of something that eats paint. Two in the morning, rain, an empty lot, and there's a night cleaner inside who'd be finishing his shift about now, and nobody upstairs has thought about him at all.

choices.consequence: You do it and get back in the car with your hands stinging and the men in the back delighted with you. The cleaner comes out as you're pulling away.
You refuse, and somebody else's headlights are already turning in. The thing absorbs your conscience without slowing down, which tells you what your part in it is worth.

nodes.text: You knew him first in the church basement: hormones, a body that betrayed him twice, crying on your shoulder about a divorce and two sons who won't call. Now he's downstairs on Paper Street in a black shirt with his head shaved, and he's happy, properly happy, and he calls you sir. He has found somewhere to put all of it. You are the reason he found it.

choices.consequence: You let him fold you up the way he did in the basement, and for a second it's the old thing, and then he says sir again and it isn't.
You get a hand up between you and watch him take the correction like a good soldier. He's better at obedience than anyone here, which is why he goes out on the first night job.

nodes.text: Cornelius. Rupert. Travis. Whatever's on the badge that week. There is a whole shelf of men you have been for an hour at a time, none of them liable for anything the others did, and it never once occurred to you to wonder where a habit like that ends up. Marla is the only person alive who has caught you at it, and she uses three different names on you in one afternoon just to watch.

choices.consequence: You stay Cornelius, because Cornelius sleeps at night and gets hugged and owes nobody anything. The rent on that is coming due and it isn't small.
You give your actual name to a stranger in a circle of folding chairs and it sounds ridiculous in your own mouth, like a word said too many times over.

nodes.text: Twenty of them on the porch in the rain, waiting three days for permission to come in, and more arriving by bus. They've shaved their heads and burned their fingerprints off with lye and they answer every question with a sentence they have all been issued. They don't want to be told they're special. They want to be told they're not, by somebody with a loud enough voice, and they'll do anything for it.

choices.consequence: You step out, say two sentences, and forty men move. It's the best feeling of your life, and it takes about a week to understand what that says about you.
You tell them to go home and they write it down as an instruction and stay precisely where they are. You have built a thing that cannot hear the word no.

nodes.text: You find the plan in a folder in the kitchen, in your own handwriting, which you decide not to examine. Twelve buildings, credit records, a whole country's debt zeroed in ten minutes. He says nobody gets hurt. He has scheduled it for a Saturday. He has a good answer ready for every objection you can think of, and the answers being good is the frightening part.

choices.consequence: You put the folder on the table and demand he explain the handwriting. He grins and asks whose hands you think those are, and doesn't wait for you to answer.
You carry two crates down and wire a timer beside a man who calls you sir, and you're competent at it, and being competent lets you avoid thinking for a whole afternoon.

nodes.text: You get the ropes on and the room is lit by one desk lamp and you start talking to him, and he answers from behind you, from beside you, from inside your own mouth. A hotel clerk in Delaware has you in the register under his name. He never once ate in front of anybody. Every phone call — every single one — happened while you were the only person in the room.

choices.consequence: You look, and the arithmetic finishes itself in about four seconds, and nine months of things you were proud of rearrange into things you did alone.
You get out of the room and down two flights and it comes with you, obviously, because it has been coming with you the whole time. Running is the only skill you kept.

nodes.text: She's on the list. Of course she's on the list — she is the only person who could have told you who you were, which makes her the one thing the arrangement can't survive. You call her from a payphone and she assumes you're being cruel again, because every previous version of you was. You have roughly ninety seconds of credibility left with her and you've already spent most of it.

choices.consequence: You tell her to get on a bus, any bus, and she asks why in a voice that has stopped pretending. It's the first honest conversation you've had with anyone.
You hang up and go do the important thing instead, and the important thing is a building, and she is a person, and you know which of those matters.

nodes.text: A parking structure and a security camera, and on the tape there is one man throwing himself down a flight of concrete steps, standing up, and doing it again. From the inside it is a war. From the outside it is the loneliest thing anybody has ever filmed. Your face swells shut on one side and you can't stop, because stopping would mean the other man was never there.

choices.consequence: You let it run until you can't stand, and there's a relief in the damage that you recognise from the basement, and you finally see what that relief has been costing.
You lie still on the concrete and say out loud, to nobody, that you can't do this any more. The garage is completely silent. That silence is the answer.

nodes.text: Wet road, two men in the back who worship him, and he takes both hands off the wheel and asks what you'd have done with your life if you had ever stopped waiting for it to start. You give a real answer and he calls it small. The oncoming lights are getting bigger. The two in the back are smiling, because they've been taught that fear is something other people have.

choices.consequence: You grab it and hold the lane, and someone in the back groans like you've spoiled a party. Wanting to live is now the unpopular position in your own car.
You let the road decide and the van goes down the embankment and nobody dies, and one of them crawls out laughing. You lie in the wet grass wanting your mother.

nodes.text: Top floor, unfinished, the city laid out below and the vans parked where they need to be. The barrel is between your teeth and it is your hand holding it and his voice staying calm. Down there somewhere is an apartment where you once cared a great deal about the colour of a sofa. You have about ninety seconds and one idea, and the idea depends on him not hearing you think it.

choices.consequence: You angle it out through your own cheek and fire, and the noise takes your hearing, and the man in the room goes down with a hole in the back of his head.
You hold still and let him talk, and he wins the argument easily, because he has had your voice the entire time and knows every exit you own.

nodes.text: They bring her up in a bag with two of the black shirts holding her arms, which is precisely how you asked for it to be done, months ago, in somebody else's voice. Then the first charge goes and the twelve towers along the block begin, very slowly, to sit down into their own footprints. There is no sound at all for about a second. Somewhere below, a night guard is on his rounds.

choices.consequence: You put a hand over her face and she pulls it off, because she has been an adult about all of this from the beginning and you still haven't started.
You hold her shoulders square to the glass and tell her it's beautiful, and hear the sentence come out in the wrong voice, and take it back far too late.

nodes.text: The men are gone. Your ears are ringing and there's a hole through your face and she has your hand, and the two of you are standing at a window watching the dust come up the avenue. You start to apologise and it comes out badly. She tells you your timing has always been appalling, and doesn't let go, and neither of those facts cancels the other one.

choices.consequence: You keep her hand and watch it happen and let yourself feel the size of what you set moving, instead of looking somewhere easier.
You take your hand back so she isn't standing next to it when the questions start. She tells you that isn't yours to decide.
You stop watching the window entirely and look at her, which is the first thing in two years you have chosen with him out of the room.

nodes.text: Twelve towers come down in eight minutes and the record of what everybody owed goes with them, and nothing is rebuilt for six years. The dust reaches the glass and the window goes brown. Marla's fingers are small and cold inside yours. You watch a city lose its books and feel almost nothing, and the almost is the part that keeps you awake later, in a room with the lock on the outside, trying to work out how much of it you meant.

A basement with a coffee urn, folding chairs, sixteen people, none of them lying about why they came. You say your actual name, and then you say the rest of it — the second man, the months, the things done in your own handwriting. Nobody hugs you. A woman two chairs along nods slowly and says she has heard something like it before, which isn't comfort exactly, but it is the first true room you have stood in.

She takes you back to the hotel she's living in, gets the bandage on properly, and puts you in a bed with a chair jammed under the door handle. Around four she asks what you're actually called. You tell her, and it is the plainest, dullest name in the world, and saying it costs you nothing and everything. She repeats it once to check she has it right. Then she uses it, and you answer to it.
